newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--U.S. price growth seen benign 1997, 1998.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--U.S. price growth seen benign 1997, 1998.

text.p: U.S. inflation should remain tame over the next two years despite an unemployment rate parked below 5.5 percent, said economists in the latest Reuters quarterly economic survey.
Forecasters at banks, securities firms, and research institutions projected, on average, that growth in the core Consumer Price Index (CPI) would read 2.7 percent in 1997 and 3.0 percent in 1998.
At the same time, they forecast a jobless rate of 5.2 percent this year and 5.3 percent in 1998.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, expanded 2.5 percent for the year ended March 1997, while the unemployment rate stood at 5.2 percent last month.

The decline in the unemployment rate during 1996 prompted price-hike fears among inflation alarmists. But judging by their forecasts, economists now are less concerned about price pressures developing in the labor market.
The common belief that higher labor costs must beget higher goods and services prices no longer rings true, said John Ryding, managing director and senior economist at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc.
"Between 1993 and the present day, there is no relationship between wages and inflation," Ryding said. "Wage increases have tended to rise, and inflation has tended to decline."

Productivity gains, as well as foreign competition arising from a strong dollar, have persuaded businesses to strive to maintain the bottom line without passing higher costs along to consumers, Ryding said.
Labor-force demographics and economic factors endemic to the current business cycle negate some previous inflation assumptions, other economists said.
Donald Ratajczak, director of the economic forecasting center at Georgia State University, said the unemployment rate may hold near 5.0 percent without straining resources.

The growth rate of the labor force is now nearly 2.0 percent, much faster than many economists had expected, and industrial capacity continues to expand at a rate of nearly 4.0 percent, double its 1993 growth rate, Ratajczak said.
"This is why so far, there's no evidence of inflation," he said.
While none of the experts projected runaway prices, a few stressed that even the 0.3 percentage-point uptick projected for core CPI between 1997 and 1998 would be worth watching.
"We do think the core (CPI) is likely to drift up in 1997 with the decline in the unemployment rate," said Paul Kasriel, chief U.S. economist at Northern Trust.
Kasriel forecast unemployment would run at 5.1 percent in 1997 and 5.2 percent in 1998, and he estimated the core CPI would edge up to about 2.8 percent by the end of this year.
Such an inflation rate would still be "benign," but could be a harbinger of future price trends, he said.
"What I'm trying to signal is not so much the (inflation) number, but the direction," Kasriel said.
In contrast with some survey respondents, Kasriel said growth in the workforce does not appear strong enough to offset rising labor demand, the economist said.
"I'm not saying wages cause inflation, but when you don't have enough people, that's a capacity constraint," Kasriel said. "That allows firms to raise their prices."
But Kasriel said inflation may remain contained, with increases in some areas offset by continued strength in the dollar and price stability in certain commodities.
Besides forecasting core CPI, the economists offered similar projections for the overall Producer Price Index (PPI). On average, they saw PPI expanding 1.7 percent in 1997 and 2.0 percent in 1998.
